profile.reading: This building is part of Microsoft's West Des Moines, Iowa data center hub, a cluster of campuses the company has built since first opening in the city in 2012. Microsoft has invested an estimated $5 billion to $6 billion across its West Des Moines facilities to date, per reporting from Wisconsin Public Radio, which visited the site while researching a comparable Microsoft project in Wisconsin, and the company now owns more than 600 acres across the metro. West Des Moines' city engineer told WPR that each Microsoft campus typically comprises three to four buildings and takes roughly eight to ten years to fully build out, which is consistent with this registry finding multiple OSM-mapped Microsoft buildings clustered along the same streets in Dallas, Polk, and Warren counties. More than 600 people now work across Microsoft's West Des Moines data centers, in roles spanning mechanical and electrical engineering, campus management, IT operations, security, and building maintenance, making Microsoft roughly the seventh- or eighth-largest full-time employer in a city of about 73,000 residents. One of the named campuses, internally called Project Osmium, sits on the south side of West Des Moines near Interstate 35; the Business Record has separately reported on a sixth Microsoft data center project, called Project Ruthenium, planned near Veterans Parkway and Woodland Avenue with an initial $210 million, 245,000-square-foot building and roughly 25 permanent jobs, part of a site that could eventually hold up to four buildings. This building sits along Grand Avenue or Booneville Road in Dallas County, in the western portion of Microsoft's West Des Moines footprint; Microsoft has not published which named campus or project this specific building belongs to, nor its individual square footage or MW capacity, consistent with the company's general practice of not disclosing per-building specifics for its Azure data centers.

reading.body:
Microsoft has not published the power capacity or square footage of this Dallas County building, which sits on the western edge of the company's West Des Moines data center hub along Grand Avenue or Booneville Road. The building is one of five completed campuses Microsoft has built in West Des Moines since 2012, with a sixth project approved for construction starting in 2026, and Microsoft has disclosed only that all West Des Moines operations run on renewable energy. The site falls within a footprint where Microsoft now owns more than 600 acres, supports more than 600 permanent employees across mechanical, electrical, IT, and facility roles, and has invested an estimated $5 billion to $6 billion to date, making it among the largest private employers in a city of 73,000 residents.

The specific building belongs to an unnamed campus or project on Microsoft's West Des Moines cluster, consistent with the company's practice of not disclosing per-building capacity figures for its Azure infrastructure. West Des Moines engineering and public reporting indicate each Microsoft campus typically comprises three to four buildings built out over eight to ten years, though this registry cannot map this particular structure to the named projects Osmium or Ruthenium without county assessor records. Iowa has only two published megawatt figures across its 52 mapped AI-relevant facilities, so most capacity in the state, including this building, remains opaque to public scrutiny.

The absence of published specifications makes this campus invisible to grid and capacity analyses despite its scale within one of the largest hyperscaler data center clusters in the United States. Its relevance to AI scaling depends entirely on what Microsoft has built here and what power it draws, neither of which the company has disclosed. To assess whether this facility matters to AI compute supply, an analyst would need to obtain building square footage from Dallas County records or power consumption data from Xcel Energy, Microsoft's regional utility provider.
